CHAPTER 3.1 · LEARNING AREA 3 · FEBRUARY · MARCH

Vectors in space

An aeroplane at an altitude of 10 km, a drone above the school yard, the corner of a roof: to give points in space you need three coordinates. Displacements, forces and velocities are described with vectors, arrows with a length and a direction. You calculate with them as easily as with numbers, and they are the tool for lines and planes in the next two chapters.

12 LESSONS3 UNITS3DHISTORY
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • represent and read off points and solids in the three-dimensional Cartesian coordinate system
  • calculate distances between two points and midpoints
  • calculate with vectors: addition, subtraction, multiples and their laws
  • interpret and check linear dependence and independence geometrically
  • use vectors for points of division, centroids and parallelograms

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1The three-dimensional coordinate system

The ceiling light hangs 4 m from one wall, 3 m from the other and 3 m high: $L(4, 3, 3)$. Its distance from the origin corner: on the floor, the point below it is $\sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = 5$ m away; together with the height, $\sqrt{5^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{34} \approx 5.83$ m. So Pythagoras' theorem also holds in space, with three squares under the root.

KEY POINT · POINTS IN SPACE

A point has three coordinates $P(x, y, z)$. The axes are pairwise perpendicular; the three coordinate planes are the $xy$ plane ($z = 0$), the $xz$ plane ($y = 0$) and the $yz$ plane ($x = 0$).

Distance between two points: $\overline{AB} = \sqrt{(x_B - x_A)^2 + (y_B - y_A)^2 + (z_B - z_A)^2}$

Midpoint: $M\!\left(\tfrac{x_A + x_B}{2}, \tfrac{y_A + y_B}{2}, \tfrac{z_A + z_B}{2}\right)$

Oblique drawing: the $x$-axis is usually drawn slanting forwards and shortened, the $y$-axis to the right and the $z$-axis upwards.

Reflecting: In the $xy$ plane only $z$ changes sign; in the origin all three coordinates do.

Software: In 3D programs and in the widget you can rotate the coordinate system. An oblique drawing shows only one view, and some points look the same in it.

INTERACTIVE · POINTS IN SPACE

Change the coordinates of $A$ and $B$ and rotate the coordinate system with the mouse or your finger. The widget shows the connecting vector, the length and the midpoint.

EXAMPLE 1 · DISTANCE AND MIDPOINT

Given $A(1, 2, 3)$ and $B(4, 6, 3)$.

$\overline{AB} = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2 + 0^2} = 5$.

$M(2.5, 4, 3)$. Both points are at height 3; the line segment is parallel to the $xy$ plane.

EXAMPLE 2 · PYRAMID

A right pyramid has the square base with the corners $(\pm 2, \pm 2, 0)$ and the height 6. How long is a lateral edge?

Apex $S(0, 0, 6)$, corner $E(2, 2, 0)$.

$\overline{ES} = \sqrt{4 + 4 + 36} = \sqrt{44}$, so $2\sqrt{11} \approx 6.63$.

EXERCISES

Which points lie on an axis, which in a coordinate plane? $(5, 0, 0)$, $(0, -2, 5)$, $(3, 4, 0)$, $(0, 0, -3)$, $(1, 1, 1)$

On axes: $(5, 0, 0)$ ($x$-axis), $(0, 0, -3)$ ($z$-axis). In planes: $(0, -2, 5)$ ($yz$), $(3, 4, 0)$ ($xy$). $(1, 1, 1)$ lies in none.

Calculate the distance from the origin: a) $(2, 3, 6)$   b) $(1, 2, 2)$   c) $(0, 0, -3)$

a) 7   b) 3   c) 3

A cuboid has the edges 3, 4 and 5 parallel to the axes. Give the coordinates of all the corners if one corner is at the origin, and calculate the space diagonal.

Corners $(0, 0, 0)$, $(3, 0, 0)$, $(3, 4, 0)$, $(0, 4, 0)$, $(0, 0, 5)$, $(3, 0, 5)$, $(3, 4, 5)$, $(0, 4, 5)$; diagonal $\sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2}$.

How far is $P(3, 4, 12)$ from the $z$-axis, how far from the $xy$ plane?

From the $z$-axis $\sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$, from the $xy$ plane 12.

On the $z$-axis there is a point $P$ that is the same distance from $A(2, 1, 0)$ and $B(0, 1, 4)$. Find it.

$P(0, 0, z)$: $4 + 1 + z^2 = 0 + 1 + (z - 4)^2 \Rightarrow 4 = -8z + 16 \Rightarrow z = 1.5$.

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Calculating with vectors

Every hour the aeroplane covers 200 km to the east, and the wind displaces it by 30 km to the south. The two displacements one after the other give a displacement diagonally to the south-east. As arrows you put them end to end; as columns of numbers you add them: $\begin{pmatrix} 200 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -30 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 200 \\ -30 \end{pmatrix}$, length $\sqrt{200^2 + 30^2} \approx 202.2$ km/h.

KEY POINT · VECTORS

A vector is the set of all arrows of the same length, parallel and pointing the same way. In space you write $\vec{a} = \begin{pmatrix} a_1 \\ a_2 \\ a_3 \end{pmatrix}$.

Position vector of $P$: $\vec{p} = \overrightarrow{OP}$ · connecting vector “head minus tail”: $\overrightarrow{AB} = \vec{b} - \vec{a}$ · magnitude: $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{a_1^2 + a_2^2 + a_3^2}$

Calculate component by component: $\vec{a} \pm \vec{b}$ and $r \cdot \vec{a}$. The commutative, associative and distributive laws hold as for numbers.

Opposite vector $-\vec{a}$, zero vector $\vec{0}$. Chain of vectors: $\overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{BC} = \overrightarrow{AC}$.

Vector quantities: displacement, velocity, force, field strength. Scalar quantities such as mass, time and temperature have no direction.

Unit vector: $\dfrac{\vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|}$ has length 1 and the same direction as $\vec{a}$.

INTERACTIVE · SUM, DIFFERENCE, MULTIPLE

Set $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ and choose “sum and difference” or “multiple”. Rotate the picture to see the arrows from all sides.

EXAMPLE 3 · CALCULATING

$\vec{a} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$, $\vec{b} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$. Calculate $2\vec{a} - \vec{b}$ and $|\vec{b}|$.

$2\vec{a} - \vec{b} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 - 3 \\ 0 - 1 \\ 4 + 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ -1 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$.

$|\vec{b}| = \sqrt{9 + 1 + 1} = \sqrt{11}$.

EXAMPLE 4 · COMPLETING A PARALLELOGRAM

$A(1, 1, 0)$, $B(4, 2, 1)$ and $C(5, 5, 3)$ are corners of the parallelogram $ABCD$. Find $D$.

In the parallelogram, $\overrightarrow{AD} = \overrightarrow{BC} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$.

$\vec{d} = \vec{a} + \overrightarrow{BC}$: $D(2, 4, 2)$.

EXERCISES

Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $|\overrightarrow{AB}|$: a) $A(1, 2, 3)$, $B(4, 0, 5)$   b) $A(1, 2, 2)$, $B(3, 5, 8)$

a) $(3, -2, 2)$, length $\sqrt{17}$   b) $(2, 3, 6)$, length 7

Solve for $\vec{x}$: a) $\vec{x} + \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$   b) $3\vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ -3 \\ 9 \end{pmatrix}$

a) $(3, -2, -2)$   b) $(2, -1, 3)$

The forces $\vec{F}_1 = (3, 0, 0)$ N, $\vec{F}_2 = (0, 4, 0)$ N and $\vec{F}_3 = (0, 0, 12)$ N act on a body. How large is the resultant force?

$\vec{F} = (3, 4, 12)$ N, $|\vec{F}| = \sqrt{9 + 16 + 144} = 13$ N.

Find the unit vector in the direction $(0, 3, 4)$ and a vector of length 10 in the same direction.

$\left(0, \tfrac{3}{5}, \tfrac{4}{5}\right)$; $(0, 6, 8)$.

Show with vectors: in every quadrilateral $ABCD$ the midpoints of the four sides form a parallelogram.

Calculate the vector between the midpoints of $AB$ and $BC$ and the one between the midpoints of $DA$ and $CD$.

$\overrightarrow{M_{AB}M_{BC}} = \tfrac{1}{2}(\vec{c} - \vec{a})$ and $\overrightarrow{M_{DA}M_{CD}} = \tfrac{1}{2}(\vec{c} - \vec{a})$: equal vectors, so a parallelogram (Varignon's theorem).

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3Linear dependence, midpoints and points of division

With the vectors $\vec{a} = (1, 2)$ and $\vec{b} = (1, -1)$ you can reach every point of the plane, for example $(5, 1) = 2\vec{a} + 3\vec{b}$. With $\vec{a}$ and $2\vec{a}$, on the other hand, only the points of a line: the two are linearly dependent. In space you need three vectors that do not lie in one plane to reach every point.

KEY POINT · LINEAR DEPENDENCE

A linear combination of $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$ is a vector $r\vec{a} + s\vec{b} + t\vec{c}$ with real numbers $r$, $s$, $t$.

Vectors are called linearly dependent if one of them can be written as a linear combination of the others; equivalently: $r\vec{a} + s\vec{b} + t\vec{c} = \vec{0}$ has a solution in which not all the numbers are zero.

Geometrically: two vectors dependent ⟺ parallel (collinear); three vectors in space dependent ⟺ they lie in one plane (coplanar).

Point of division: $T$ divides $AB$ in the ratio $m : n$ if $\vec{t} = \vec{a} + \tfrac{m}{m + n}\overrightarrow{AB}$. Centroid of a triangle: $\vec{s} = \tfrac{1}{3}(\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c})$.

Quick test for two vectors: is every component of one the same multiple of that of the other? $(2, 4, -6) = 2 \cdot (1, 2, -3)$: parallel.

Three points on one line? Check whether $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$ are collinear.

INTERACTIVE · QUADRILATERALS IN SPACE

Move the corners of a quadrilateral. Using vectors, the widget checks whether opposite sides are parallel and equally long.

EXAMPLE 5 · COLLINEAR?

Do $A(1, 2, 3)$, $B(2, 4, 5)$ and $C(4, 8, 9)$ lie on one line?

$\overrightarrow{AB} = (1, 2, 2)$, $\overrightarrow{AC} = (3, 6, 6) = 3 \cdot \overrightarrow{AB}$.

Yes, and $B$ divides $AC$ in the ratio $1 : 2$.

EXAMPLE 6 · THREE VECTORS

Are $(1, 0, 0)$, $(0, 1, 0)$ and $(1, 1, 0)$ linearly dependent? And $(1, 1, 0)$, $(0, 1, 1)$, $(1, 0, 1)$?

First: $(1, 1, 0)$ is the sum of the others, and all lie in the $xy$ plane: dependent.

Second: $r + t = 0$, $r + s = 0$, $s + t = 0$ only has $r = s = t = 0$: linearly independent.

EXERCISES

Are the vectors parallel? a) $(2, 4, -6)$ and $(1, 2, -3)$   b) $(1, 2, 3)$ and $(2, 4, 5)$   c) $(2, -4, 6)$ and $(-1, 2, -3)$

a) yes   b) no   c) yes, in opposite directions

Find $B$ if $M(1, 1, 1)$ is the midpoint of $A(3, 0, -1)$ and $B$.

$\vec{b} = 2\vec{m} - \vec{a} = (-1, 2, 3)$

Find the centroid of the triangle $A(1, 0, 0)$, $B(0, 3, 0)$, $C(2, 0, 6)$ and the point that divides $AB$ from $A$ in the ratio $1 : 2$.

$S(1, 1, 2)$; $T = A + \tfrac{1}{3}\overrightarrow{AB} = \left(\tfrac{2}{3}, 1, 0\right)$.

For which $r$ is $(3, r, 6)$ parallel to $(1, 2, 2)$? Write $(4, 5, 6)$ as a linear combination of $(1, 1, 0)$, $(0, 1, 1)$, $(1, 0, 1)$.

$r = 6$. $(4, 5, 6) = 1.5 \cdot (1, 1, 0) + 3.5 \cdot (0, 1, 1) + 2.5 \cdot (1, 0, 1)$.

Is the triangle $A(1, 1, 1)$, $B(3, 1, 1)$, $C(2, 3, 1)$ isosceles? Is the quadrilateral $ABCD$ with $D(0, 3, 1)$ a parallelogram?

$|\overrightarrow{AC}| = |\overrightarrow{BC}| = \sqrt{5}$: isosceles. $\overrightarrow{AB} = (2, 0, 0)$, $\overrightarrow{DC} = (2, 0, 0)$: yes, a parallelogram.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A cube with edge length 4 has one corner at the origin and lies in the region with only positive coordinates. Give the opposite corner and the length of the space diagonal.

$(4, 4, 4)$, diagonal $\sqrt{48} = 4\sqrt{3} \approx 6.93$.

Connecting with Chapter 2: Checking for linear independence is a homogeneous system of equations. Write it as a matrix for $(1, 1, 0)$, $(0, 1, 1)$, $(1, 0, 1)$ and solve it with Gauss–Jordan elimination.

$\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \vec{x} = \vec{0}$ leads to the identity matrix: only $\vec{x} = \vec{0}$, so independent.

A drone starts at $(0, 0, 0)$ (in m), flies $(30, 40, 0)$, then $(0, 0, 20)$, then $(-10, 0, 10)$. Where is it, and how far is it from the start?

$(20, 40, 30)$, distance $\sqrt{400 + 1600 + 900} = \sqrt{2900} \approx 53.9$ m.

Show that the space diagonals of a cuboid intersect in one point and bisect each other there.

With one corner at the origin and edges $a$, $b$, $c$: all four diagonals have the midpoint $\left(\tfrac{a}{2}, \tfrac{b}{2}, \tfrac{c}{2}\right)$.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

A formula on a bridge

On 16 October 1843 the Irish mathematician William Rowan Hamilton was walking with his wife along the Royal Canal in Dublin. For years he had been looking for a way to calculate with points in space, just as you can calculate with complex numbers in the plane. On Brougham Bridge the solution came to him, and he carved the formula $i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = ijk = -1$ into the stone. This gave rise to the quaternions, and in these years Hamilton also coined the word vector, Latin for “carrier”.

Almost at the same time, in 1844, the Stettin grammar school teacher Hermann Grassmann published his “Lineale Ausdehnungslehre” with a general calculus of line segments in any number of dimensions. It was so far ahead of its time that hardly anyone understood it. Today it is the foundation of linear algebra.

Sources: Hamilton's letter on the discovery: Trinity College Dublin, School of Mathematics, “Letters describing the discovery of quaternions”. Sources differ on whether he introduced the word “vector” in 1843 or only in 1846. H. Grassmann, “Die lineale Ausdehnungslehre”, Leipzig 1844. The original inscription has not survived; a plaque commemorates it.
